SPMS Athletic Field Remediation.current_status: The South Portland Middle School athletic field is safe and ready for use. Following a remediation plan involving aeration, overseeding, and fertilization, the field was declared ready for fall sports in August 2026.
overview: On August 17, 2026, the administration confirmed that the SPMS field was safe and ready for fall soccer and field hockey after successful remediation.
The Director of Operations outlined a specific spring remediation plan involving aeration, overseeding, and fertilization on January 12, 2026.
On December 8, 2025, the Buildings & Grounds Committee was noted to be reviewing the ongoing issue with the unusable athletic field.
The administration detailed the field's problems with soil quality and compaction and proposed a remediation plan on November 3, 2025, while the board discussed contractor accountability.
On October 6, 2025, middle school staff and coaches raised significant concerns that the athletic field had been unusable for nearly four years due to its rocky and uneven condition.

Board: Discussed holding the original contractor financially responsible for the field's failures (November 3, 2025).
Raised the ongoing issue of the unusable field during a committee report (December 8, 2025).
Administration: Confirmed the field was safe and ready for fall sports after successful remediation (August 17, 2026).
Presented a spring remediation plan to address soil compaction, rocks, and funding (January 12, 2026).
Reported on issues with soil quality and compaction and outlined a multi-step remediation plan (November 3, 2025).
Staff: Described the field as rocky, uneven, and unusable for nearly four years (October 6, 2025).
Reported that the poor field condition led to a loss of coaching staff, practice space, and impacted the athlete pipeline (October 6, 2025).

Student Cell Phone Policy 2026.current_status: The board has formally adopted and implemented a new 'away for the day' cell phone policy for the 2026-2027 school year. The administration reports a successful launch at secondary schools while addressing parent safety concerns.
overview: On September 14, 2026, the board unanimously passed the second read of the rules, formalizing the policy, and the administration reported a successful launch.
On August 17, 2026, the board approved the first reading of the implementation rules, which vary by grade level for storing devices from bell-to-bell.
On July 20, 2026, the board discussed the state-mandated policy, clarifying that administrators were still developing the specific implementation procedures for board review.
On June 8, 2026, the board held the first read of a state-mandated cell phone policy that prohibits phone use during the school day and planned a public workshop.

Board: Unanimously passed the second read of the rules for personal electronic devices on September 14, 2026.
Approved the first reading of the implementation rules on August 17, 2026.
Held a public workshop to help develop procedures for the new policy.
Administration: Reported a successful launch of the new policy at secondary schools.
Developed grade-level specific rules for device storage, including main office storage, lockers, and morning lockboxes.
Addressed parent safety concerns related to the new policy.
Citizens: Some parents raised safety concerns regarding the new policy.

SPHS Athletic Complex.current_status: The South Portland High School Athletic Complex project is currently in the design phase. It is reportedly on time and on budget for a planned groundbreaking in May 2027.
overview: On September 14, 2026, the Buildings & Grounds Committee reported that the project had entered the design phase.
Athletic Director Todd Livingston reported on August 17, 2026, that the project was on time and on budget for a May 2027 groundbreaking.

On April 14, 2025, the board rescinded its prior action and voted to send two conflicting referendum questions to voters with updated costs, allowing a choice between natural grass and synthetic turf.
The board had previously passed a substitute motion on February 24, 2025, to send a two-choice referendum to the city council, an action that was later reversed.
In a series of workshops in January 2025, the board and public debated the costs, environmental impacts, and playability of synthetic turf versus natural grass options.
The renewed discussion began after a citizen group spoke against artificial turf on December 9, 2024, citing health and environmental research.

Board: Expressed a strong preference in April 2025 for two conflicting referendum questions to ensure a fair and democratic process.
Debated the long-term financial commitment and environmental impact of synthetic turf, including PFAS and microplastics, in January 2025.
Questioned the historical neglect of the fields and whether all alternatives had been fully explored during a January 2025 workshop.
Passed the initial two-choice referendum motion in February 2025 with a narrow 4-3 vote following a tense debate.
Administration: The Superintendent presented revised, higher costs in April 2025 due to previously missed line items like general conditions and contractor overhead.
The Superintendent presented a compromise plan in January 2025 involving two synthetic turf fields and one grass field.
On January 8, 2025, Tim Metheny presented a revised proposal to reduce the amount of synthetic turf and total project cost.
Athletics Director Todd Livingston argued for synthetic turf in January 2025 to increase playability and reduce weather-related cancellations.
Staff: Some staff argued in April 2025 against any spending on athletics given the district's budget shortfall and the need to fund academic and support positions.
Citizens: Offered varied perspectives in April 2025, with some opposing any spending on athletics while others urged letting voters decide on the long-delayed upgrades.
Voiced strong opposition to artificial turf in February 2025, citing environmental impacts, long-term costs, and the tax burden on residents.
Presented opposing views in January 2025, with some citing environmental and health risks of turf while others emphasized the need for durable, high-usage fields for student-athletes.
An advocacy group spoke against artificial turf in December 2024, requesting to be included in the board's study of the issue.

Student Enrollment and Class Size.current_status: The district is addressing high kindergarten enrollment at Small Elementary School by adding a new classroom in a portable building. This action comes as overall district enrollment saw a slight year-over-year increase, though the long-term trend remains downward.
overview: On August 17, 2026, the administration added a new kindergarten classroom in a portable building at Small Elementary School to manage high enrollment.
Timothy Matheney highlighted a significant 7% decline in district enrollment and its potential financial impact on September 9, 2024.
On May 13, 2024, Timothy Matheney reported a steady decline in student enrollment and warned that it will impact future state subsidies and present financial challenges.

Administration: Reported a slight year-over-year enrollment increase of 20 students, though the long-term trend points downward.
Added a new kindergarten classroom at Small Elementary School by utilizing a portable building to address high enrollment.
Previously warned that declining enrollment will impact state subsidies and create future financial challenges.
Staff: A teacher raised safety and security concerns about using portable classrooms compared to the main school building.
Citizens: A middle school student and his mother called for greater peer respect, kindness, and mental health support in schools.

Elementary School Reconfiguration.current_status: The board has decided against a major elementary school reconfiguration at this time. Instead, it is pursuing the superintendent's recommendations to develop a proposal for an early learning center, create a committee for differential school funding, and commission an external review of special education programming.
overview: On November 9, 2026, the board reversed its direction on reconfiguration, instead approving the superintendent's recommendation to explore an early learning center, differential school funding, and a special education review.
The Elementary Reconfiguration Committee presented two final options to the board on November 2, 2026: maintaining current K-4 boundaries or creating a grade-banded K-2 and 3-4 system.
On April 29, 2026, the board voted to delay the implementation of any elementary reconfiguration until the 2027-2028 school year to allow for more thorough planning.
The board had originally voted 4-2 on March 30, 2026, to adopt a grade-banded reconfiguration model for the remaining elementary schools following the decision to close Kaler Elementary.

The process began on February 9, 2026, when the board voted to request a formal proposal from the superintendent on reconfiguring the elementary schools as a potential cost-saving measure amid budget challenges.
Initial discussions about redrawing attendance zones to address significant demographic and resource disparities between elementary schools began as early as October 2024.

Board: Unanimously approved the superintendent's November 2026 recommendation to halt reconfiguration and pursue alternative equity strategies.
Expressed disappointment in the final map options presented in November 2026, questioning if they truly solved the district's equity problems.
Initially voted 4-2 in March 2026 to adopt a grade-banded model, believing it was the best path to equity despite a rushed timeline.
Directed the administration in March 2026 not to close Skillin Elementary, citing the impact on the west end community.
Administration: On November 9, 2026, Superintendent Dr. Angola Atkinson Duina recommended against a major reconfiguration, citing a need for stability.
In November 2026, Assistant Superintendent Dr. Johanna Prince presented the committee's final two map options and a proposal for an early learning campus at the former Kaler school.
Initially, in March 2026, the administration strongly advocated for a grade-banded reconfiguration as the best way to improve equity and resource allocation.
Staff: In November 2026, teachers raised health concerns about using Kaler as an early learning center and highlighted significant resource inequities at Skillin Elementary.
In April 2026, union leaders and teachers voiced strong opposition to the rushed reconfiguration plan, calling for a pause.
During the initial March 2026 debates, many teachers expressed support for reconfiguration to improve equity, while others urged a slower, more deliberate process.
Citizens: In November 2026, community members from Protect South Portland raised serious health and safety concerns about reopening Kaler School due to its proximity to oil tanks.
Parents expressed relief when the reconfiguration was delayed in April 2026, but some argued the delay prolonged inequity, especially for the Kaler community.
During the initial March 2026 debates, parents were divided between prioritizing neighborhood school stability and seizing the opportunity for systemic change to address inequity.
Throughout the process, parents and community members consistently called for more transparency, better communication, and a slower, more thoughtful decision-making process.

Assistant Superintendent Compensation.current_status: The board is facing significant public backlash after unanimously approving a one-time twelve thousand dollar retirement contribution for Assistant Superintendent Dr. Jo Prince. While the board defended the decision as recognition for her extensive extra work, staff and community members have criticized the move as tone-deaf in light of recent budget cuts and layoffs.
overview: On June 8, 2026, the Board Chair defended the board's recent un-agendized vote to award a twelve thousand dollar retirement contribution to Assistant Superintendent Dr. Jo Prince.
During the June 8, 2026 meeting, community members and staff strongly criticized the compensation decision, calling it tone-deaf in the wake of school closures and staff layoffs.

On June 4, 2026, the board voted unanimously to approve the one-time twelve thousand dollar retirement contribution to Dr. Jo Prince in recognition of her extensive work on school reconfiguration and the budget.

Board: Board members supported the contribution to recognize the Assistant Superintendent's extensive work on the budget, labor contracts, and school reconfiguration.
The Board Chair defended the vote against public criticism, citing the administrator's heavy workload during a challenging year.
Staff: Staff and union representatives expressed disappointment, arguing the compensation decision showed a lack of shared sacrifice during layoffs and budget freezes.
Citizens: Parents and citizens criticized the un-agendized vote as a slap in the face given the closure of Kaler Elementary and cuts to student programs.

Education Foundation.current_status: A committee is actively forming a new South Portland Schools Education Foundation. They are developing a mission and board, and have partnered with the University of Maine Law School to establish 501(c)(3) nonprofit status.
overview: On December 8, 2025, citizens and the SPTA president reiterated community interest in establishing a district education foundation.
On November 3, 2025, SPMS Principal Dr. Rebecca Stern reported that a committee was forming the foundation, developing its mission, and working with legal partners to secure nonprofit status.

Administration: SPMS Principal Dr. Rebecca Stern provided an update on the formation of the new education foundation.
Citizens: Citizens and the SPTA president expressed support and reiterated community interest in establishing an education foundation.

Superintendent Transition 2026.current_status: The board has appointed Andy Wallace as a short-term interim superintendent to cover a two-week gap in July. Mr. Wallace declined a salary for the role and will receive vacation days as compensation.
overview: On June 4, 2026, the board appointed Andy Wallace as interim superintendent for two weeks in July to cover the gap between the outgoing and incoming superintendents.

Board: Appointed an interim superintendent to ensure leadership continuity during the transition.
Administration: Interim appointee Andy Wallace declined a salary for the short-term role, accepting four vacation days as compensation instead.

Director of Operations and Safety Resign.current_status: The Director of Operations and Security, Mike Nalli, has resigned from his position. The Board of Directors accepted the resignation with regret, praising his significant contributions to district safety.
overview: On June 4, 2026, the superintendent announced the resignation of Mike Nalli, the Director of Operations and Security, which the board accepted with regret.

Board: Expressed regret over the resignation, calling it a significant loss.
Praised Nalli's contributions to improving district safety and his reliability in handling urgent situations.
Administration: The superintendent formally announced the resignation to the board.

FY26 Budget.current_status: The district is projected to close the FY26 budget with a minimal deficit, a significant improvement from earlier projections. However, this outcome leaves the district with virtually no fund balance, raising concerns about its ability to handle future financial emergencies.
overview: On September 14, 2026, the Finance Committee reported that the district is projected to close the FY26 budget with a minimal deficit but no remaining fund balance.
A non-personnel spending freeze implemented in December 2025 was credited in a July 20, 2026 report with improving the budget's outlook from a previously projected deficit of up to $1.1 million.
The Board approved the over $73 million FY26 budget on June 3, 2025, following a contentious process that included significant proposed cuts to staff and administrative positions.
On March 31, 2025, the board failed to vote on the proposed budget due to deep divisions over its contents, including a controversial proposal to freeze administrator salaries.
The initial FY26 budget proposal, presented in March 2025, included the elimination of approximately 20 positions to close a multi-million dollar gap caused by declining enrollment and rising costs.
As early as May 13, 2024, the administration warned that declining student enrollment would create significant financial challenges for the FY26 budget cycle.

Board: Expressed concern over the lack of a fund balance after closing the budget with a minimal deficit.
Showed significant division during budget development, including a split vote on the final instruction budget and a failed motion to approve the budget in a prior meeting.
Rosemarie DeAngelis voted against the Regular Instruction budget line to protest cuts to social-emotional learning funding.
Questioned the administration's rationale for cutting the Director of Curriculum position while retaining other newer director roles.
Administration: Implemented a non-personnel spending freeze in late 2025 to mitigate a projected multi-million dollar deficit.
Framed the budget as a necessary 'right-sizing' in response to a 15-year low in student enrollment.
Proposed eliminating approximately 20 positions, including the Director of Curriculum, to balance the budget.
Strongly opposed a proposed salary freeze for top administrators, arguing it was disrespectful and damaging to leadership.
Staff: Reported that the district's spending freeze forced teachers to use personal funds for classroom supplies.
Strongly opposed proposed cuts to student-facing positions, particularly in social-emotional learning, multilingual support, and curriculum.
Supported a proposed salary freeze for top administrators as a way to preserve jobs for student-facing staff.
Criticized the administration for a perceived lack of transparency and for damaging trust during the budget development process.
Citizens: Expressed concern that closing the fiscal year with no fund balance was irresponsible.
Voiced strong opposition to cutting student-facing positions, arguing the administration was 'top-heavy' and the process lacked transparency.
Argued against spending on athletics while academic and support positions were being cut.
Urged the board to provide better community education on budgetary issues.

Kaler Elementary School Closure.current_status: The closure of Kaler Elementary is proceeding as planned at the end of the 2025-2026 school year. The board has approved a modified end-of-year schedule to facilitate the move and is arranging district-funded childcare for affected families.
overview: On June 4, 2026, the board approved a modified end-of-year schedule for Kaler to accommodate its closure and committed to providing childcare for families impacted by the change.
The board postponed a decision on Kaler's end-of-year schedule on May 27, 2026, to ensure adequate time for parent feedback.
During the April 13, 2026 meeting, citizens expressed frustration that the Kaler closure was proceeding even though a broader district reconfiguration plan had been delayed.
The board voted 6-1 on March 30, 2026, to approve the closure of Kaler Elementary School, citing declining enrollment and the need for operational savings.
On March 23, 2026, the administration first presented the proposed closure of Kaler Elementary as a central part of the district's budget options.

Board: Voted 6-1 to close Kaler Elementary to achieve operational savings and prevent deeper staff cuts.
Approved a modified end-of-year schedule to facilitate the school's closure.
Delayed a vote on the schedule to allow for more parent feedback.
Administration: Initially proposed closing Kaler as part of two budget options to address declining enrollment.
Reported that community-building efforts, including open houses and PTA collaboration, were underway to welcome Kaler families.
Committed to working with community partners to provide free childcare for families affected by the modified school calendar.
Staff: Kaler's interim principal and staff expressed relief at having a clear timeline to plan for the closure and their future placements.
Many teachers and staff passionately argued against the closure, criticizing the rushed process and its impact on students.
Over 90% of Kaler teachers supported the modified end-of-year schedule to facilitate the move.
Citizens: Kaler parents highlighted the profound and inequitable impact of the closure on their vulnerable student population.
Many parents and community members voiced concerns about the rushed timeline, lack of transparency, and emotional toll on students.
Dozens of citizens gave emotional testimony against the closure and related budget cuts during public comment.
Some expressed frustration that the closure was proceeding while other reconfiguration plans were delayed, prolonging inequity.

Superintendent Appointment 2026.current_status: Dr. Angola Atkinson Duina has been officially appointed as the new superintendent and has begun her tenure. She has provided her first report to the board, outlining her entry plan and initial activities.
overview: On July 20, 2026, the board officially welcomed new Superintendent Dr. Angola Atkinson Duina, who provided a report on her first days and entry plan.
The board unanimously approved the contract for Dr. Angola Atkinson Duina as the new superintendent on May 27, 2026.

Board: Unanimously approved the new superintendent's contract.
Officially welcomed Dr. Angola Atkinson Duina at her first meeting.
Administration: Dr. Angola Atkinson Duina expressed her honor and excitement to join the district upon her contract approval.
Provided a report on summer work, leadership meetings, and an entry plan to build relationships and understand district needs.

Kaler Elementary Student Placement.current_status: The board has approved the administration's plan to reassign Kaler Elementary students to the district's four remaining elementary schools. A robust and prioritized waiver process will be utilized for affected families, with transportation options for waived students to be explored.
overview: On May 27, 2026, the board passed the Kaler student attendance proposal on a 5-1 vote after reconsidering the motion, emphasizing the need for a waiver process.
During the May 27, 2026 meeting, an initial vote on the student reassignment plan failed due to a 3-3 tie.
Assistant Superintendent Dr. Jo Prince presented the administration's proposal on May 27, 2026, which was designed to balance class sizes, capacity, and demographics.
At the same meeting, several Kaler parents voiced strong opposition to the plan during public comment, calling it divisive and a betrayal.

Board: Members were initially divided, leading to a failed 3-3 vote on the proposal.
Some opposed the plan for splitting neighborhoods and burdening Kaler families.
The final 5-1 vote to approve the plan was driven by the need to move forward with planning and to implement a robust waiver process.
Administration: Assistant Superintendent Dr. Jo Prince presented the plan to reassign Kaler students to the four other elementary schools.
The proposal aimed to balance class sizes, building capacity, and demographics while keeping student groups and siblings together.
Citizens: Kaler parents, including Doug Von Werssowetz, strongly opposed the reassignment plan.
Parents described the proposal as shortsighted, divisive, and a betrayal of the Kaler community.

Superintendent Search 2026.current_status: The board has authorized negotiations with its preferred superintendent candidate following a search process that narrowed the field to two finalists. An official announcement is pending the completion of these negotiations.
overview: On May 11, 2026, the board authorized its chair to enter negotiations with the preferred candidate for the superintendent position.
The board announced two finalists for the superintendent role and scheduled a community meet-and-greet for May 6th, as noted on April 29, 2026.
On February 9, 2026, the board made a one-time exception to policy to allow student representatives to participate in confidential semi-finalist interviews.
A board member noted low attendance at a virtual forum and urged broader community participation in feedback sessions during the February 4, 2026 meeting.
The board approved contracts with the search firm Zeal for national advertising and comprehensive background checks on January 12, 2026.
After hearing from three firms, the board voted 4-2 on December 10, 2025, to hire ZEAL Education Group to facilitate the superintendent search.

Board: Debated the high cost of the chosen search firm, Zeal, against its perceived benefits of a comprehensive, board-centric process.
Expressed concern over low public attendance at early feedback forums.
Valued Zeal's expert guidance, national reach, and process designed to build board consensus.
Administration: Strongly criticized the board's decision to conduct a closed search process, arguing it damaged public trust.
Staff: Argued that excluding key stakeholders from the search committee devalued the community's voice.
Citizens: Voiced strong criticism during public comment regarding the closed search process and lack of stakeholder inclusion on the search committee.

FY27 Budget.current_status: The FY27 budget, which includes a 6% tax increase, was approved by the City Council and is scheduled for a final voter referendum on June 9, 2026. Following criticism of the timeline, the board has already amended the calendar to begin the next budget cycle earlier.
overview: On June 8, 2026, the board voted to amend the 2026-27 meeting calendar to begin the budget process in December, responding to public criticism that the FY27 process started too late.
The Director of Finance reported on May 11, 2026, that the budget was approved by the City Council and will go to voters for final approval on June 9th.
On April 29, 2026, the Board gave final approval to the FY2027 operating budget, which included a 6% tax increase and the restoration of several positions using one-time funding.

The board voted 4-2 on April 7, 2026, to adopt the Superintendent's Budget and advance it to the City Council, using newly found insurance savings to restore some positions and create a contingency fund.
On March 30, 2026, the board initially rejected the Superintendent's FY27 budget proposal in a 2-5 vote, citing concerns over specific cuts and the rushed nature of the process.

The budget process began with the administration presenting a projected $7-8 million shortfall in early 2026, proposing significant structural changes including the reduction of over 70 staff positions and a potential elementary school closure.

Board: Initially rejected the administration's budget proposal due to concerns about the speed of the process and specific cuts.
Sought additional financial support and guidance from the City Council to mitigate cuts and build a contingency fund.
Ultimately passed a revised budget to provide certainty to staff, while also voting to start the next budget cycle earlier in response to public feedback.
Debated the necessity of large structural changes, with some members expressing concern about revisiting contentious issues like school reconfiguration.
Administration: Proposed major structural changes, including significant staff reductions and school reconfiguration, to address a large, ongoing deficit.
Recommended reclassifying director-level roles into instructional strategists to achieve cost savings while retaining expertise.
Advocated for creating a new contingency fund to build long-term financial stability for the district.
Argued that realistic budgeting for non-personnel costs was essential to protect staff positions from future cuts.
Staff: Union representatives and teachers consistently spoke out against cuts to student-facing roles in related arts, special education, and mental health.
Highlighted critical safety and staffing shortages in special education classrooms and the resulting low morale among educators.
The SPTA President urged the board to avoid a process that pitted staff against each other and offered collaboration.
Expressed deep concern over the rushed process and the impact of proposed cuts on specific programs like music.
Citizens: Parents and students passionately opposed cuts to programs they deemed vital for student well-being and engagement, such as art, music, and physical education.
Many expressed deep concern over the scale of the proposed cuts and the potential closure of a neighborhood school, criticizing the rushed process.
Some residents urged the board to request a higher tax increase from the City Council to avoid the most drastic reductions.
Public criticism of the budget timeline directly led the board to amend the calendar for the following year's process.

Special Education Staffing.current_status: The district is facing critical safety and staffing shortages in special education classrooms due to recent budget cuts. Staff, union representatives, and the public have voiced significant concerns about the impact on students and educator morale.
overview: On April 7, 2026, teachers and union presidents highlighted severe safety and staffing shortages in special education classrooms during public comment.
The administration detailed budget cuts on March 23, 2026, which included reductions to special education staff as part of a larger 12% cut to district personnel.
During the March 23, 2026 meeting, an extensive public comment period featured passionate debate from students, parents, and teachers over cuts to special education programs.

Administration: Detailed the notification process and specific number of reductions across all unions, including special education.
Staff: Highlighted critical safety and staffing shortages in special education classrooms.
Expressed concerns about low morale and the loss of vital support positions.
Spoke passionately against cuts to special education programs.
Citizens: Passionately debated specific cuts to special education programs during public comment.

Dyer Elementary School Closure.current_status: The administration has proposed closing Dyer Elementary School as part of the budget plan, citing higher facility repair costs compared to Kaler Elementary. The proposal is currently under debate by the board and has drawn significant public concern regarding health and safety.
overview: On March 9, 2026, the administration proposed closing Dyer Elementary School, citing higher projected facility repair costs than Kaler Elementary.
During the March 9, 2026 meeting, the board and public debated the community impact, student displacement, and the criteria used for the closure decision.
Public commenters at the March 9, 2026 meeting raised significant health and safety concerns about keeping Kaler Elementary open, noting its proximity to petroleum tanks.

Board: Debated the community impact, student displacement, and criteria used for the closure decision.
Administration: Stated the decision to close Dyer over Kaler was based on higher projected facility repair costs for Dyer.
Citizens: Raised health and safety concerns about keeping Kaler Elementary open, citing its proximity to petroleum tanks and potential for VOC exposure.
Contrasted Kaler's industrial location with Dyer's larger green space and safer setting.

Skillin Elementary School Closure.current_status: The administration has proposed closing Skillin Elementary as one of several cost-saving scenarios. However, the Board has directed the administration to cease exploring this option and focus on alternatives due to concerns about equity and the impact on west end families.
overview: On March 2, 2026, the Board directed the administration to stop considering the closure of Skillin Elementary and to instead focus on other restructuring models.
The administration presented scenarios on March 2, 2026, that included closing either Skillin or Kaler elementary schools to achieve fiscal savings and improve educational equity.

Board: Expressed strong opposition to closing Skillin, citing the disproportionate impact on the west end's marginalized and lower-income populations.
Directed the administration to explore closing other schools like Kaler or Dyer, or alternative redistricting.
Administration: Recommended scenarios involving the closure of either Skillin or Kaler to achieve savings and improve equity.
Proposed reconfiguring remaining schools into grade-level bands as part of the restructuring.

Community School Model.current_status: The board has unanimously approved a district-wide expansion of the community school model, beginning with the high school. This decision follows a successful implementation at South Portland Middle School that showed improved student outcomes.
overview: On February 9, 2026, the board unanimously voted to expand the community school model district-wide, starting with the high school, to better integrate academic, health, and social services for students.

On October 15, 2024, the leadership of the South Portland Middle School Community School presented their successful model and proposed its expansion across the district with a sustainable funding plan.

Board: Voted unanimously to expand the community school model district-wide after seeing positive results at the middle school.
Administration: Presented on the success of the SPMS model, highlighting improved attendance, engagement, and academic outcomes.
Proposed a district-wide expansion to integrate academics, health services, and family engagement for all students.

SPHS Graduation Venue.current_status: The 2025 SPHS graduation ceremony will remain at the high school's Martin Field. Based on recent survey results, the district is strongly considering a move to a larger, climate-controlled venue for the 2026 ceremony.
overview: On January 13, 2025, the high school principal presented survey results and confirmed the 2025 ceremony would remain at Martin Field, with a move to a larger venue strongly considered for 2026.
Survey results presented on January 13, 2025, identified Cross Insurance Arena as a top choice for its capacity and weather certainty.
On November 12, 2024, the board decided to survey students and families for input on moving the graduation ceremony to a larger, indoor venue to accommodate more guests and avoid weather issues.

Board: Initiated discussion to move the ceremony to a larger, indoor venue.
Sought to avoid weather-related cancellations and accommodate more family members.
Requested a survey of students and families for input.
Administration: Presented survey results on potential future graduation venues.
Recommended keeping the 2025 ceremony at Martin Field.
Noted that a move to a larger venue is being strongly considered for 2026.
Citizens: Survey results indicated a preference for Cross Insurance Arena for its capacity and weather certainty.

SPESPA Collective Bargaining.current_status: Negotiations between the district and the South Portland Educational Support Professionals Association (SPESPA) are at an impasse, with the union having sought a mediator. SPESPA cites dangerously low staffing levels for Ed Techs as a primary concern.
overview: On October 14, 2026, the SPESPA president announced the union had sought a mediator for negotiations due to frustrations over low staffing levels and budget cuts.
During the November 3, 2025 meeting, multiple union leaders urged the board to quickly settle the contract for educational support professionals.
The board voted on May 30, 2024, to enter an executive session to discuss collective bargaining with SPESPA.

Board: Voted unanimously on May 30, 2024, to enter an executive session to discuss collective bargaining with SPESPA.
Staff: SPESPA President Connie DiSanto stated the union has sought a mediator due to frustrating negotiations over dangerously low staffing levels.
The union has been open to temporary solutions like subcontracting to address staffing shortages.
Union leaders have urged the board to extend the same urgency to SPESPA negotiations as to other contracts.

Extended Learning Opportunities Program.current_status: The Extended Learning Opportunities (ELO) program is ongoing at South Portland High School through a partnership with JMG. The board recently received a positive update on the program, which included a student presentation.
overview: On December 8, 2025, the board received an update on the Extended Learning Opportunities program as part of the Superintendent's report, which featured a student presentation.
On March 28, 2024, the district announced that the ELO program would continue through a new partnership with JMG, which will provide a full-time "ELO Navigator" to run the program.
On March 25, 2024, the Superintendent committed to finding an alternative staffing and funding solution to continue the ELO program after its state grant expired.

Board: Expressed strong support for continuing the ELO program on March 25, 2024.
Requested more details on the ELO transition plan before the final budget vote.
Members DeAngelis and Ryan advocated for exploring a dedicated grant writer position for programs like ELO.
Administration: Announced a partnership with JMG on March 28, 2024, to ensure the ELO program's continuation.
Committed on March 25, 2024, to finding a way to continue the valued program after its grant funding expired.
Citizens: A parent shared a letter from their graduate son on March 25, 2024, detailing how the ELO program provided him a career path in firefighting and urging its continuation.

SPTA Contract 2025-2028.current_status: The board has unanimously ratified the new three-year contract with the South Portland Teachers’ Association (SPTA). The agreement concludes a lengthy negotiation process that had progressed to the fact-finding stage.
overview: On November 3, 2025, the board unanimously voted to ratify the new three-year contract with the SPTA.
On October 6, 2025, the board was in the fact-finding stage of negotiations and heard extensive public comment from teachers, parents, and community members advocating for a fair contract.
On September 8, 2025, the board held an executive session to discuss confidential labor negotiations with the South Portland Teachers Association.

Board: Expressed relief and gratitude for reaching an agreement after a lengthy process.
Stated a commitment to a fair resolution while negotiations were ongoing.
Staff: Union representatives expressed relief and gratitude upon reaching an agreement.
Advocated for a fair contract with retroactive pay and protections for seniority and leave, citing financial hardship, professional stress, and feeling undervalued.
Citizens: Dozens of parents and community members voiced strong support for the teachers' union, urging the board to settle the contract.

Concussion Management Policy.current_status: The board is refining Policy JJIF to enhance parental notification and involvement in return-to-play decisions. The policy was sent back to committee for further work following the most recent discussion.
overview: On September 8, 2025, the board voted to send proposed changes to the concussion policy back to committee for refinement, seeking to ensure parents are included in return-to-play decisions.

Board: Focused on ensuring parents are notified and included in the decision-making process for a student's return to play.
Voted to send the policy back to committee for further refinement.

School Calendar 2026-2027.current_status: The first reading of the 2026-2027 school calendar has been postponed. The board is negotiating with the service employees' union regarding the impact of a proposed additional school day.
overview: On January 12, 2026, the board voted to postpone the first reading of the 2026-2027 school calendar to negotiate with the service employees' union.

Board: Voted to postpone the calendar's first reading to allow for union negotiations.
Staff: The service employees' union requires negotiations over the impact of an additional school day.

SPHS Athletic Field Referendum.current_status: The district is weighing the tax implications of natural grass versus synthetic turf for the proposed SPHS athletic field referendum. Public input has been received on the options while the project moves forward.
overview: On October 6, 2025, the Athletic Director presented the estimated first-year tax impact for both the natural grass and synthetic turf options for the high school athletic field referendum.

Administration: Athletic Director Todd Livingston presented the estimated tax impacts for both the natural grass and synthetic turf options.
Citizens: Some members of the public expressed support for the overall project but advocated for the natural grass option due to environmental and cost concerns with synthetic turf.

Educational Equity Policy.current_status: The board has unanimously approved a new Educational Equity Policy. This policy provides a framework for using data to identify and address inequities within the district.
overview: On June 8, 2026, the board unanimously approved the new Educational Equity Policy.
The board approved the first read of the new Educational Equity Policy on May 11, 2026, advancing it for a second read.

Board: Unanimously approved the policy's first read and final adoption, indicating strong support.
Administration: The district's equity committee developed the policy to guide data review and address inequities.

SPMS Athletic Field Referendum.current_status: The board has approved revised wording for the upcoming municipal referendum on the SPMS athletic field. The changes are intended to clarify the choice between a natural grass field and a synthetic turf field for voters.
overview: On August 18, 2025, the board approved revised wording for the municipal referendum to clarify the choice between a natural grass field and a synthetic turf field.

Board: Voted to approve revised referendum wording to prevent voter confusion.

Board Leadership Change.current_status: Tandy Ratliff serves as the Board Chair. Following the resignation of the previous vice chair, Tyler Smith was unanimously elected to the position on April 13, 2026.
overview: On April 13, 2026, the board unanimously elected Tyler Smith as the new Vice Chair following the announced resignation of Adrian Dowling.
On August 18, 2025, the board elected Rosemarie DeAngelis as the new Vice Chair and Chair Tandy Ratliff announced she would not be seeking re-election.
On July 14, 2025, Tandy Ratliff was unanimously elected as the new Board Chair during a time of administrative transition.

Board: Discussion during the August 2025 vice chair election centered on board leadership precedent and the need for stability.
Members praised Tandy Ratliff's temperament, experience, and dedication upon her unanimous election as chair.

SPESPA Grievance.current_status: The Board of Education has unanimously denied a grievance from the South Portland Educational Support Staff Professionals Association (SPESPA). This decision was made following an Executive Session on January 8, 2025.
overview: On January 8, 2025, the board unanimously voted to deny a grievance from the South Portland Educational Support Staff Professionals Association (SPESPA) following an Executive Session.

Board: Unanimously voted to deny the SPESPA grievance.
Staff: The South Portland Educational Support Staff Professionals Association (SPESPA) filed a grievance that was ultimately denied.

Tobacco-Free Schools Policy.current_status: The board has given final approval to the Tobacco-Free Schools Policy. The policy is now officially adopted by the district.
overview: On January 8, 2024, the board gave final approval to the policy concerning tobacco-free schools as part of a larger consent agenda.

Board: The board unanimously approved the final policy.

Special Education.current_status: The board has approved a recommendation from the superintendent to commission an external review of the district's special education programming. This action is part of a broader set of initiatives aimed at district stability and improvement.
overview: On November 9, 2026, the board unanimously approved commissioning an external review of the district's special education programming.
On March 25, 2024, the Director of Instructional Support provided an overview of the department, which serves 649 students with disabilities, and detailed the IEP and Child Find processes.

Board: Unanimously approved the superintendent's recommendation for an external review of special education programming on November 9, 2026.
Administration: On November 9, 2026, Superintendent Dr. Angola Atkinson Duina recommended commissioning an external review of special education programming.
Director Kat Cox and her team presented an overview of the Instructional Support department and its services on March 25, 2024.
Citizens: Spoke in strong support of the Special Education department during the March 25, 2024 meeting, sharing personal stories of its positive impact.

Public Participation Policy.current_status: The board has approved changes to the public participation policy, which eliminates the ability for speakers to yield their time to another person. The new policy was passed on a 4-2 vote and is now in effect.
overview: On October 14, 2026, the board held a second reading and voted 4-2 to approve the revised public participation policy, eliminating the practice of yielding time.
The board held a first reading of proposed changes to the public participation policy (BEDH) on September 14, 2026, which included eliminating time-yielding and setting a 10:00 PM meeting end time.

Board: The final vote was split 4-2, indicating division on the issue.
Some members supported the change as a necessary step.
Other members argued the change unnecessarily limits the public's voice.
Citizens: Public comment occurred at both meetings where the policy was discussed.
The proposed changes sparked debate during public comment at the September 14, 2026 meeting.

Differential School Funding.current_status: The board has approved the creation of an ad hoc committee to explore differential funding for schools with higher needs. This action follows a recommendation from the superintendent and testimony from staff about resource inequities.
overview: On November 9, 2026, the board unanimously approved establishing an ad hoc committee to explore differential funding for schools with higher needs.

During the November 9, 2026 meeting, Superintendent Dr. Angola Atkinson Duina recommended creating the committee as part of a broader plan to address district challenges without a major elementary reconfiguration.
Teachers from Skillin Elementary detailed significant inequities in the allocation of MTSS staff and resources at the November 9, 2026 meeting, urging the board to address the disparities.

Board: Unanimously approved moving forward with the superintendent's recommendation to establish a committee to explore differential funding.
Administration: Superintendent Dr. Angola Atkinson Duina recommended creating a committee for differential school funding to address needs while maintaining stability.
Staff: Teachers from Skillin Elementary detailed significant inequities in MTSS staff and resource allocation compared to other schools, urging the board to address the issue.

Immigration Enforcement.current_status: The board has unanimously voted to recommend that the City Council include the School Department in a city-wide ordinance limiting cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. This decision prioritizes the stronger legal protection of an ordinance over a standalone school policy.
overview: On October 26, 2026, the board voted unanimously to recommend the City Council include the School Department in a city-wide ordinance on immigration enforcement, reasoning that an ordinance provides more legal strength than a policy.
During the January 12, 2026 meeting, citizens and staff called for accelerated training and clearer protocols to protect vulnerable families from ICE activity.
On January 27, 2025, the Superintendent reaffirmed that schools are safe zones and outlined the district's plan to support immigrant families in response to federal policy changes.

Board: Unanimously supported inclusion in the city ordinance, believing it provides more legal strength than a policy.
Argued the symbolic message of unity and protection was crucial and outweighed potential jurisdictional risks.
Administration: Dr. Angola Atkinson Duina explained the School Department is developing its own policy (KLGC) to comply with state law.
Presented differing legal opinions, noting the School Department's counsel advised against inclusion in the city ordinance, citing the board's exclusive authority.
Previously reaffirmed that schools are places of learning, not enforcement, and committed to providing resources and training for staff.
Staff: Called for accelerated training and clearer protocols to protect vulnerable families from ICE activity.
Citizens: Public commenters, including parents and activists, unanimously urged the board to recommend inclusion in the city ordinance.
Argued a legally binding ordinance offers greater protection for students, staff, and families than a school policy.
Previously called for clearer protocols and faster training to protect families.
